newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. durable goods orders seen up in Dec.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. durable goods orders seen up in Dec.

text.p: U.S. orders for costly manufactured goods likely rebounded in December, bolstered by increased demand for products such as machinery, home appliances and apparel, experts said.

December durable goods orders were expected to be up 1.2 percent after tumbling 1.6 percent in November, based on the average forecast of economists polled by Reuters. Data are due out Wednesday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Part of the gain is simply a "snap-back" from the decline in the previous month, said Leonard Santow, a managing director at Griggs and Santow Inc.
Santow said he expects modest gains in electrical and non-electrical machinery, transportation and primary metals.
Experts paid particular attention to electrical machinery orders which plunged 9.3 percent in November.
Orders for durable goods which includes cars and home appliances that last at least three years reflect the vitality of the manufacturing sector, a key component of the overall economy.
"I think consumer durables other than autos will probably do reasonably well," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
"Manufacturing is picking up because, I think, they are getting more orders from non-auto durable goods like appliances and apparel," Sohn said.
Experts termed durable goods a volatile series in which the aircraft component is especially erratic.
Transportation equipment orders were unchanged in November after falling a revised 6.8 percent in October.

Ian Shepherdson, chief U.S. economist at HSBC Markets, noted that the "big unknown" that is effecting the durable goods numbers now and possibly for the next few months is the American Airlines order for Boeing aircraft.
"There is an added element of volatility in what is already an extremely volatile series," Shepherdson said.

News first emerged last November that American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, had agreed to buy more than $6.0 billion worth of Boeing Co. jetliners. The airline had said when it placed the order that making the order final would be contingent on a new labor pact with the carrier's pilots.
In light of the erratic nature of the aircraft component, experts tend to strip it out to get a more accurate reading of how durable goods orders are faring in the wider economy.
"My inclination is to look only at the ex-transportation series which is trending up quite nicely, and I'd expect it to strengthen again over the next few months," Shepherdson said.
He attributed this partly to domestic demand and to strength in exports, which he predicted will not last.
"I think that the strength in the dollar ... will slow down exports quite significantly this year," he added.
